title: Iran says two more tankers hit mines in Hormuz as Trump vows war will end 'one way or the other'
dek: The Revolutionary Guards say a supertanker is on fire after a mine strike on an 'unauthorised route'. The claims are unverified, and mediators in Doha are still working on a two-day plan to reopen the strait before Tuesday's US midterms.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Sunday night that two oil tankers had exploded after striking Iranian naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, one of them a supertanker it said was "engulfed in flames". The claim, carried by Iran's state broadcaster, could not be independently verified, and neither ship has been named.

The incident, the latest in a week of reported mine strikes, came hours before US President Donald Trump said again that the war with Iran would end "very soon, one way or the other", and two days before Americans vote in midterm elections that both Washington and Tehran have treated as a turning point. Mediators in Doha are still working on an Iranian plan to reopen the strait within two days.

## What happened

A spokesperson for the IRGC Navy told the state broadcaster IRIB that the two tankers had been "in violation of regulations" and were using "an unauthorized route" through the strait when they hit mines, The Jerusalem Post reported. According to the statement, as reported by Iran's Press TV and republished by Orinoco Tribune, both ships had switched off their navigation and identification systems to pass "covertly", and both were "brought to a halt at the scene". The IRGC said the vessels were operating with US military support, a claim for which it gave no evidence, and said their owners "shall bear full responsibility".

Earlier on Sunday, an IRGC statement said Iran's regular navy had struck and destroyed an "enemy vessel" east of the strait, the Jerusalem Post reported. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO), which is run by the Royal Navy and tracks attacks on shipping, said a tanker had been hit by an "unknown projectile" on Sunday, after the master of a nearby ship reported the strike. It was not clear whether that ship was one of the two in the IRGC statement.

Accounts differ on the details. Anadolu Agency, in a report carried by Malaysia's The Star, said the IRGC had announced on Saturday that a single supertanker struck a mine in "an unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz"; Press TV described Sunday night's statement as covering two tankers. The IRGC has given no ship names, flags or crew figures for any of the weekend's incidents, and no shipowner, flag state or the US Central Command had confirmed them by early Monday India time. CENTCOM has previously said the main transit routes are clear of mines, a claim Iranian officials have called "baseless propaganda", according to Press TV.

The IRGC said any vessel that turns off its identification systems in the strait will be treated as a threat.

## Background

Iran has now claimed at least six mine strikes on tankers since Friday: four on Friday and Saturday, according to its own statements reported by Gulf News, and the two announced on Sunday night. None has been confirmed by an independent source. Over the same period, the Qatari liquefied natural gas carrier Al Mayeda, with six Indian sailors aboard, was hit by "unidentified objects" in the Gulf, and Oman evacuated 25 crew from a burning Panama-flagged tanker off its Musandam peninsula.

The UKMTO has recorded 81 projectile attacks on ships in the strait since 6 July, 59 of them on the southern route, CBS News reported. The US says its blockade of Iranian oil shipments has redirected 144 vessels.

The fighting began on 28 February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran. A ceasefire followed in April, and a US-Iran memorandum on freedom of navigation was signed in June, but its implementation stalled, Anadolu reported, and Al Jazeera said it had collapsed by August. Since then the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been the main front.

## What they are saying

Trump said the war would be over "very soon, one way or the other", and that Iran would either agree a deal or "we'll just end it", Al Jazeera reported. On Saturday he said the US still had to "take care of" one or two Iranian sites, including the underground complex known as Pickaxe Mountain, but that he was "not in a hurry". Iran denies carrying out nuclear work there.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Qatari and Pakistani mediators were "continuing consultations regarding our conditions", and that he hoped the US would have "enough sense to choose diplomacy", Al Jazeera reported. Iran's plan would reopen the strait within two days if Washington lifts recent sanctions, restores oil waivers granted in June, reduces its forces in the region, recognises shipping routes designated by Iran and Oman, and ends the conflict on all fronts, including Israel's attacks on Lebanon.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said talks led by Qatar were continuing. "Talks have actually never stopped," he said, adding that the US would be open to a diplomatic solution, according to Al Jazeera. He has also said Trump has not decided whether to order new strikes.

Iran's army spokesman, Mohammad Akraminia, warned on state television on Sunday that a new war "could last longer" than the last one, AFP reported, according to CBS News.

> "For now, diplomacy and military preparations are proceeding simultaneously." – Hamidreza Azizi, Crisis Group, quoted by Al Jazeera

Al Jazeera reported that the US had warned Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense round of fighting after the midterms, and that a senior Israeli official, cited by the Israeli news site Ynet, said Israel was preparing for another round immediately after the vote. Neither government has said so publicly.

## Markets

Oil prices eased in early Asian trade on Monday as Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks, Reuters reported, with Brent crude down about 1.5% at around $111.7 a barrel, after it settled at $113.43 on Friday and rose 13.6% over October. Asian shares were also lower, weighed down by worries about the cost of the artificial-intelligence investment boom.

## What it means for India

India buys most of its crude oil abroad, and a large share of its oil and gas imports normally passes through Hormuz, so every reported strike feeds into fuel prices and the import bill. Thousands of Indian sailors also work on ships in the Gulf. The Ministry of External Affairs has said 22 Indian nationals, 14 of them seafarers, have been killed in the West Asia conflict, ANI reported. The government said last week that Indian crew on three ships hit near the strait were all safe; no Indian nationals have been reported aboard the ships named in Sunday's claims.

## What happens next

Americans vote on Tuesday, 3 November. Trump said in October that the US would not attack Iran before the midterms. Whether Washington accepts Iran's two-day plan, rejects it, or resumes strikes once the vote is over is now the main question for shipping and for oil importers such as India.

## Key numbers

- Tanker mine strikes claimed by Iran since Friday: at least six, none independently confirmed
- Projectile attacks recorded by UKMTO in the strait since 6 July: 81
- Indian nationals killed in the West Asia conflict, per the MEA: 22, including 14 seafarers
- Brent crude: about $111.7 in early Asian trade on Monday, down about 1.5%
- US midterm elections: Tuesday, 3 November
